_readme: U15 — accuracy under load: the twelve highest-frequency local error areas. Subject-verb agreement (basic and hard), the three prepositions of time and place plus dependent prepositions and prepositional adverbials, the whole punctuation cluster (sentence boundaries, commas, semicolon/colon/apostrophe), adverb placement, -ed and -ing adjectives, dummy it and there, and the confusable pairs.
Punctuation is scored inside Grammatical Range and Accuracy in Writing and is almost never taught, so gr_comma_rules, gr_comma_splice and gr_punctuation_rest carry the largest banks in the block.

Sequence indices are provisional band values in the range 1600-1699; tools/content/reseq_grammar.py re-seats the whole pack into 1..154. Within the band the order is topological: gr_prepositions_core before its two dependents, gr_sv_agreement_core before gr_sv_agreement_hard, gr_comma_splice before gr_comma_rules before gr_punctuation_rest.

No point in this block declares role choice: none of the nineteen closed confusion sets covers agreement, punctuation, prepositions, adverb placement or the confusable pairs, and a set with one member is not a contrast. Twin-paired choose_form items are used inside the accuracy banks instead, so the meaning-carrying choice is still drilled.

Every point declares structure_slug null. None of these has a shape the sidecar detectors in D4 can look for, so produce items carry required_structure null and are graded on the four binary checks against the prompt.

points.title: Saying when and where with in, on and at

point_json.grammar_name: in / on / at for time and place

teach.can_do: I can put in, on and at in front of a time or a place without guessing.
teach.why_it_matters: They appear in nearly every sentence you will ever write about your life, and getting one wrong is visible to a reader immediately.
teach.meaning: These three are about size, not about vocabulary. In puts something inside something with edges: a country, a town, a month, a year. On puts it on a surface or along a line: a road, a floor, a named day. At pins it to a single point: a doorway, a building on a journey, a moment on the clock. Time copies space exactly, which is why one set of three does both jobs.

form.pattern: in + the big one · on + the surface or the named day · at + the exact point
notes: in: countries, towns, months, years, seasons, and parts of the day (in the morning)
on: roads, floors, days and dates (on Tuesday, on 3 March)
at: buildings on a route, addresses with a number, clock times, at night, at the weekend
no preposition at all before this, last, next and every: the survey closed last Friday
form.negative: The preposition does not change when the sentence goes negative: the depot is not on Verdon Road.
form.question: Is the office on Verdon Road or at number forty?

spec.label: how big is the thing after the preposition?

steps.gloss: something with edges you can be inside: in Sandmouth, in April
a surface or a line you sit along: on Verdon Road, on Tuesday
one point with no width: at the depot, at ten past six

worked_example.sentence: The night bus leaves from the stop on Verdon Road at ten past eleven.
worked_example.why_this_form: A road is a line you sit along, so it takes on. A clock time is one point in the day with no width, so it takes at.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: In Verdon Road would put the stop somewhere inside the road surface, and on ten past eleven would treat a bare moment as something with a top to stand on.

notice_set.sentence: Rana lives on Brackenfield Road.
notice_set.question: Do we know her house number?
notice_set.why: On puts her somewhere along the road and never picks a point on it, so the number stays unsaid.

notice_set.sentence: Rana lives at 14 Brackenfield Road.
notice_set.question: Do we know her house number?
notice_set.why: At pins her to one point, and here the number is that point.

notice_set.sentence: The depot closes at six.
notice_set.question: Could you arrive at half past six and still get in?
notice_set.why: Six is one moment, and the doors are shut from that moment onwards.

notice_set.sentence: The roadworks will finish in August.
notice_set.question: Do we know which day they finish?
notice_set.why: In wraps the whole month round the event without choosing any day inside it.

notice_set.sentence: The market runs on Saturdays.
notice_set.question: Is the market open on Sunday?
notice_set.why: On names the day the market runs. Nothing here says anything at all about the other days.

teach.rule_line: Ask how big it is: inside takes in, along takes on, one point takes at.
teach.false_rule: That the three have to be memorised place by place. Size decides them, and time copies space.

errors.wrong: The training starts in Monday.
errors.right: The training starts on Monday.
errors.why_it_happens: In has been stored as the default time preposition because it works for months and years, and a day of the week is filed away as just another time word.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: in becomes on.

errors.wrong: We arrived in the station just before nine.
errors.right: We arrived at the station just before nine.
errors.why_it_happens: A station is a large building, so being inside it feels like the true description. English is describing the journey instead, and on a journey a station is one point.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: in becomes at.

errors.wrong: The exhibition opens at next week.
errors.right: The exhibition opens next week.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner knows a time phrase usually needs a preposition in front and supplies one by reflex. Next, last, this and every already do that job themselves.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: at.

pays_in.note: Every answer about your day, your area or your journey needs all three.
pays_in.model: I get to the depot at about eight, and on Fridays I'm there a bit earlier.

pays_in.note: A letter carries dates, times and addresses in almost every line.
pays_in.model: I moved into the flat on Brackenfield Road in March.

pays_in.note: Form-filling answers turn on hearing at, on and in correctly.
pays_in.model: The coach leaves from stand four at quarter past two.

used_in.quote: The complaint has to name the stop, the road and the time waited, which is all three prepositions inside one sentence.

payload.sentence: I'll wait for you at the ticket barrier.
payload.question: Do we know exactly where to stand?

feedback.why_key: At marks one point with no width, so the barrier is the whole of the meeting place and there is nothing left to arrange.
feedback.feed_forward: Read at as a pin in a map rather than as a general area.

payload.sentence: The new health centre is in Ashfield.
payload.question: Do we know which road it is on?

feedback.why_key: In wraps a whole district round the building and picks nothing inside it, so the road is still missing.
feedback.feed_forward: Notice how much of the map each preposition hands you.

payload.context: A colleague is explaining her hours to a new starter.
payload.sentence: I start at seven on Mondays and Thursdays.
reasons: a clock time needs in rather than at
a named day needs in rather than on
the days have been put in the wrong place
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Seven is a point on the clock and Monday is a named day, so at and on are each sitting where they belong.
feedback.feed_forward: Check each preposition against the size of the word straight after it.

payload.context: A note on the college noticeboard about term-time opening.
payload.stem: The library closes ___ eight during term time.

expected: at

feedback.why_key: Eight is a single moment on the clock, and a moment with no width takes at.
feedback.feed_forward: Reach for at whenever the time is a point rather than a stretch.

payload.context: The opening line of a letter to a landlord.
payload.stem: I have lived ___ 12 Brackenfield Road since March.

expected: at

feedback.why_key: The number turns the road into one exact point, and one exact point takes at rather than on.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for a house number before you choose between on and at.

payload.context: Tell a friend when and where the coach goes from.

expected: the coach leaves from the depot at six on sunday

feedback.why_key: Place comes before time in English, and inside the time part the clock point comes before the named day.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the place first, then the smaller time unit, then the bigger one.

payload.given: The interview is 12 May. It is ten in the morning.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that gives both, each with the right preposition.

expected: at ten in the morning on 12 may
on 12 may at ten in the morning
at ten in the morning on 12th may
on 12th may at ten in the morning

feedback.why_key: A date is a named day, so it takes on; ten is a clock point, so it takes at; the morning is a stretch with edges, so it takes in.
feedback.feed_forward: Set each time word beside its own size before you write it.

payload.audio_text: We're meeting at the depot on Friday, not in town.

expected: we're meeting at the depot on friday not in town
we are meeting at the depot on friday not in town
were meeting at the depot on friday not in town

feedback.why_key: All three are unstressed and squashed in speech, so the only way to catch them is to know which size of word is coming next.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the word after the preposition and let its size confirm what you heard.

payload.sentence: The results will be published in Tuesday morning.

expected: on tuesday morning

feedback.why_key: In the morning takes in, but once a named day is attached the day wins and the whole phrase moves to on.
feedback.feed_forward: Let the named day decide the preposition whenever one is present.

payload.context: A line from a confirmation email sent by a guesthouse.
payload.sentence: Breakfast is served in the terrace from seven.
reasons: a flat open surface takes on rather than in
the time needs at rather than from
the meal has been put in the wrong place
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A terrace has a floor and no walls, so you stand on it. In would put the guests inside the stonework.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the place has edges you can be inside before choosing in.

payload.context: Two lines taken from different letters about the same firm.
sentences: The office is on Verdon Road.
The office is at 40 Verdon Road.
meanings: Somewhere along that road, and the writer is not saying where.
One exact building, and its number is the address.

feedback.why_key: The road is the same in both. On spreads the office along it and at drops it onto a single doorstep.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose at only when you can point at one door.

payload.prompt_text: Describe how you get to work or college. Write one sentence that names the time you leave and the road or the stop you use.

feedback.why_key: One ordinary sentence about your own journey needs a place preposition and a time preposition side by side, which is where the mixing usually starts.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the place part first, then the time part.

payload.prompt_text: Take the letter of complaint about the bus service. Write the paragraph that says where you waited and for how long, then check every preposition against the size of the word after it. Six minutes.

feedback.why_key: A complaint is dense with stops, roads, dates and clock times, so it forces every one of the three into the same short paragraph.
feedback.feed_forward: Underline each preposition and name the size of the word after it.

points.title: Making the verb match how many you are talking about

teach.can_do: I can make the verb agree with the subject in an ordinary short sentence.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the most-counted small error in marked writing, it costs nothing to fix, and it is fully under your control once you know where to look.
teach.meaning: English asks the verb to say how many the subject is, but only in a few places. In the present simple the verb takes an -s when the subject is exactly one thing, and nothing when it is more than one. The verb be goes further and changes shape three ways. Everywhere else the verb keeps quiet, which is why the marked forms are easy to forget and easy to spot.

form.pattern: one thing → verb + s · more than one thing → bare verb
notes: be is the one that changes most: I am, she is, they are, it was, they were
have splits too: one has, more than one have
after does, doesn't and did, the -s comes off the main verb: she doesn't work Fridays
a modal never takes -s: the scheme can fail, never cans
the past simple marks nothing at all except in was and were
form.negative: The -s moves onto the auxiliary in a negative: the depot does not open on Sundays.
form.question: Does the depot open on Sundays? — again the -s sits on the auxiliary, not on the main verb.

spec.caption: The -s is on the noun or on the verb, never on both at once.

worked_example.sentence: The depot opens at six and the offices open at nine.
worked_example.why_this_form: One depot pulls the -s onto opens. Two or more offices leave open bare, because the noun is already carrying the plural.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The depot open would leave the reader waiting for a plural subject that never arrives, and the offices opens would suggest a single office wearing a plural name.

notice_set.sentence: The bus leaves from stand four.
notice_set.question: How many buses are being talked about?
notice_set.why: Leaves carries the -s, and on a verb the -s means exactly one.

notice_set.sentence: The buses leave from stand four.
notice_set.question: How many buses are being talked about?
notice_set.why: The -s has moved onto the noun, so the verb goes bare and the sentence is about a group.

notice_set.sentence: The staff were told on Friday.
notice_set.question: Is this about the past?
notice_set.why: Were is the past of be, and be is the one verb that keeps marking number in the past.

notice_set.sentence: My manager doesn't work weekends.
notice_set.question: How many managers are being talked about?
notice_set.why: The -s has moved onto does, which is where it always goes once an auxiliary turns up.

notice_set.sentence: The two depots handle the same volume of freight.
notice_set.question: How many depots are being talked about?
notice_set.why: Handle is bare, and a bare present-simple verb points at a subject of more than one.

teach.rule_line: One thing takes the -s on the verb; more than one leaves the verb bare.
teach.false_rule: That -s always means more than one. On a noun it does; on a verb it means exactly one.

errors.wrong: My brother work at the freight depot.
errors.right: My brother works at the freight depot.
errors.why_it_happens: The -s carries no meaning a listener needs, so it is the first thing dropped when attention goes to the content of the sentence.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: an s on work.
errors.l1_note: Many languages mark the person on the verb far more heavily, or not at all.

errors.wrong: The two schemes costs the council very little.
errors.right: The two schemes cost the council very little.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has learned that -s and singular go together and applies the marking to the whole sentence rather than to one word in it.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on costs.

errors.wrong: She doesn't works on Saturdays.
errors.right: She doesn't work on Saturdays.
errors.why_it_happens: The -s is stored as belonging to she rather than to whichever verb comes first, so it is written twice once an auxiliary appears.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on works.

errors.wrong: The report are ready for the meeting.
errors.right: The report is ready for the meeting.
errors.why_it_happens: Be is irregular enough that its forms are learned as separate words, and the link back to the number of the subject is broken.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: are becomes is.

pays_in.note: Part 1 is almost entirely present simple about your own life.
pays_in.model: My sister works nights, so she sleeps while the rest of us are out.

pays_in.note: Generalisations in an essay are present simple from start to finish.
pays_in.model: Employers expect flexibility, and a four-day week gives them very little of it.

pays_in.note: The -s is often the only clue to whether one thing or several is meant.
pays_in.model: The office opens at nine but the depots open an hour earlier.

used_in.quote: Every answer on this card is a present-simple statement about one person or one workplace.

payload.sentence: The lift runs from six in the morning.
payload.question: How many lifts are there?

feedback.why_key: Runs carries the -s, and on a verb that ending points at exactly one thing.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the ending on the verb as a count, not as decoration.

payload.sentence: The evening courses run from September to May.
payload.question: How many courses are there?

feedback.why_key: The -s has moved onto courses, so run stays bare, and a bare present-simple verb means a group.
feedback.feed_forward: Check which word is wearing the -s before you count.

payload.context: Answering a question about what your family does.
payload.sentence: My brother drives a delivery van and I work in an office.
reasons: the first verb should be bare
the second verb is missing its ending
the two halves need different tenses
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: One brother pulls the -s onto drives, and I never takes it, so both verbs are already matched.
feedback.feed_forward: Match each verb to its own subject, not to the sentence as a whole.

payload.context: From a paragraph about how a small firm is run.
payload.stem: The manager ___ (check) the orders before they leave the yard.

expected: checks

feedback.why_key: There is one manager, so the counting job falls to the verb and the -s goes on.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the subject, count it, then write the verb.

payload.context: From a description of a bar chart on freight.
payload.stem: The three routes ___ (carry) almost the same tonnage each year.

expected: carry

feedback.why_key: Routes is already carrying the plural, so the verb has nothing left to say and stays bare.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave the verb bare once the noun has taken the -s.

payload.context: Explaining your working week to somebody you have just met.
payload.stem: My shift ___ (not start) until two on Wednesdays.

expected: doesn't start
does not start
dosent start
doesnt start

feedback.why_key: Once an auxiliary turns up it takes the counting job, so does wears the -s and start goes bare.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the -s on the first verb only.

payload.context: Build one sentence about what a college provides.

expected: the college offers two evening courses every term

feedback.why_key: The college is the one thing doing the offering, so offers takes the -s even though courses just after it is plural.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the verb to the doer, not to the nearest noun.

payload.given: The new machine sorts the parcels overnight.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so that the firm has two machines.

expected: sort the parcels overnight

feedback.why_key: Once the noun goes plural the verb has nothing left to count, so the -s comes straight off.
feedback.feed_forward: When you pluralise the subject, strip the verb back.

payload.audio_text: My colleague works nights and her flatmates work days.

expected: my colleague works nights and her flatmates work days

feedback.why_key: The two verbs are the same word and the only audible difference is a hiss on the end of the first one.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the hiss on the verb and count the subject from it.

payload.sentence: Phones in classrooms distracts everybody, including the teacher.

expected: distract

feedback.why_key: Phones is the doer and it is plural, so the verb goes bare. Classrooms sitting next to it is not the subject.
feedback.feed_forward: Cover the words between the subject and the verb, then read it again.

payload.context: From an early draft of an essay about the four-day week.
payload.sentence: Many employers don't works out the real cost before they agree to it.
reasons: the ending has been written on both verbs at once
the subject should be singular
the tense is wrong for a general statement
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Don't already carries the counting job. Works is trying to do it a second time, and one sentence only needs it once.
feedback.feed_forward: After don't, doesn't or didn't, always write the bare verb.

payload.prompt_text: Write two sentences about what you do and what the people around you do: one about a single person and one about a group.

feedback.why_key: Putting the two counts side by side is what makes the ending visible, because nothing else in the sentence changes.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the subject, count it out loud, then write the verb.

payload.prompt_text: Take the Part 1 card about your work or study. Answer four of the questions out loud, then play the recording back and mark every present-simple verb whose subject is one person.

feedback.why_key: The ending is the first thing that disappears under speaking pressure, and hearing your own gaps is what makes it stick.
feedback.feed_forward: Play it back and count the endings you dropped.

points.title: Keeping the verb matched when the subject gets long

teach.can_do: I can find the real subject inside a long noun phrase and match the verb to it.
teach.why_it_matters: Agreement errors climb sharply as sentences get longer, so they are the price of the complex sentences that lift a band, and they are avoidable.
teach.meaning: Once a subject grows past two words, the verb stops sitting next to the thing it answers to. English does not care what noun is nearest; it cares which noun the sentence is actually about. Everything between that noun and the verb is scenery. A short list of quantity words then overrides the count you would expect, and there is and there are look forward instead of back.

form.pattern: find the head noun → count that noun only → match the verb to it
notes: a phrase in between never changes it: the cost of the new defences has risen
a relative clause in between never changes it: the survey that produced these figures was funded locally
each and every are one, however many nouns follow: each of the schemes has failed
a number of takes a plural verb; the number of takes a singular one
neither ... nor and either ... or match whichever part sits nearest the verb
a collective noun (the government, the team, the committee) takes a singular verb when it acts as one body and a plural one when the members act separately
there is and there are match the first item in the list that comes after them
form.negative: The rule does not change under negation: the cost of the defences has not risen since April.
form.question: In a question the auxiliary comes first and still matches the head noun: has the cost of the defences risen?

left.role: the head of the subject, which the verb answers to

right.role: everything sitting in between, which it ignores

spec.caption: The verb reaches back over the second box and matches the first.

worked_example.sentence: The cost of the new flood defences has risen twice since the survey.
worked_example.why_this_form: One cost is the thing that rose. Defences is inside a phrase explaining which cost, and a phrase like that never gets a vote.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Have risen would make the defences themselves the thing that went up, which turns a budget sentence into a sentence about sea walls getting taller.

notice_set.sentence: The list of protected sites has grown again.
notice_set.question: What has grown?
notice_set.why: Has points back to a single thing, and the only single thing available is the list.

notice_set.sentence: A number of residents have objected to the plan.
notice_set.question: How many people objected?
notice_set.why: A number of is a way of saying several, and the verb follows the several rather than the word number.

notice_set.sentence: The number of complaints has fallen since March.
notice_set.question: What is the sentence measuring?
notice_set.why: The number of names one figure, and one figure is what has fallen.

notice_set.sentence: Each of the three schemes was funded separately.
notice_set.question: Were the schemes funded together?
notice_set.why: Each takes the group apart and looks at the members one at a time, which is why the verb is singular.

notice_set.sentence: There is a car park, two cycle racks and a bus stop outside.
notice_set.question: How many car parks are there?
notice_set.why: There is matches the first item on the list, and the first item is a single car park.

notice_set.sentence: The committee are still arguing about the wording.
notice_set.question: Is the group acting as one body here?
notice_set.why: Arguing needs more than one person, so the plural verb tells you the members are acting separately.

teach.rule_line: Cover everything between the subject and the verb, then read it again.
teach.false_rule: That the verb matches the nearest noun. It matches the noun the sentence is about, however far back that sits.

errors.wrong: The impact of rising sea levels are already visible on this coast.
errors.right: The impact of rising sea levels is already visible on this coast.
errors.why_it_happens: By the time the writer reaches the verb, the last thing in working memory is levels, and the verb is matched to whatever is still warm rather than to the head noun.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: are becomes is.

errors.wrong: The survey that produced these figures were funded by the council.
errors.right: The survey that produced these figures was funded by the council.
errors.why_it_happens: A relative clause reads like a complete sentence of its own, so its last noun feels like a fresh subject when the main verb finally arrives.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: were becomes was.

errors.wrong: Each of the proposals have been costed separately.
errors.right: Each of the proposals has been costed separately.
errors.why_it_happens: Each is about a group, so it feels plural. Its whole job is the opposite: it walks through the group one member at a time.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: have becomes has.

errors.wrong: There is several reasons why the scheme stalled.
errors.right: There are several reasons why the scheme stalled.
errors.why_it_happens: There is has been learned as a fixed opener rather than as a verb that still has to look forward at what follows it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: is becomes are.

errors.wrong: Neither the council nor the residents was consulted.
errors.right: Neither the council nor the residents were consulted.
errors.why_it_happens: Neither sounds negative and singular, so it seems to set the count for the whole subject. English lets the part nearest the verb decide instead.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: was becomes were.

pays_in.note: Long subjects are what an essay is made of, and they are where agreement breaks.
pays_in.model: The effect of these measures on household bills is harder to predict.

pays_in.note: The number of and a number of sit in almost every data description.
pays_in.model: The number of journeys made by bicycle rose steadily across the period.

pays_in.note: The verb tells you which noun a long subject is really about.
pays_in.model: The range of species recorded at the reserve has narrowed since 2015.

used_in.quote: Answers on this prompt run on long subjects such as the effect of fertiliser run-off on river life.

payload.sentence: The quality of the rivers around Marlow has improved since 2018.
payload.question: What has improved?

feedback.why_key: Has points back to one thing, and quality is the only single noun in the subject.
feedback.feed_forward: Let the verb tell you which noun the sentence is about.

payload.sentence: The number of households in the district has doubled.
payload.question: Is the sentence about a total or about the households themselves?

feedback.why_key: The number of names one figure, and the singular verb keeps the reader looking at that figure rather than at the houses.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the number of as one measurement.

items.decision_cue: The share of journeys made on foot

payload.context: A line from a description of a bar chart.
payload.sentence: The share of journeys made on foot rises sharply after 2019.
reasons: the verb has been matched to the wrong noun
the phrase in the middle needs a different preposition
the tense is wrong for a chart
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: One share is what rises. Journeys sits inside a phrase saying which share, so it never gets a vote.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the head noun first, then stop reading.

payload.context: From a paragraph about farm run-off in the Verdon.
payload.stem: The effect of these chemicals on river life ___ (be) still being measured.

expected: is

feedback.why_key: Effect is the head of the subject and there is one of it. Chemicals and life are both inside phrases describing which effect.
feedback.feed_forward: Cover everything after of and read the subject again.

payload.context: From a table description about rents across four districts.
payload.stem: A number of tenants ___ (pay) more than half their income in rent.

expected: pay

feedback.why_key: A number of is a quantity word meaning several, so the tenants are what the verb answers to.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a number of as several and the verb follows.

payload.context: From an essay paragraph about tuition costs.
payload.stem: Each of the four proposals ___ (leave) graduates paying for longer.

expected: leaves

feedback.why_key: Each takes the four apart and looks at one at a time, so the verb answers to a single proposal.
feedback.feed_forward: Treat each and every as one, whatever follows them.

payload.context: Open a paragraph that will list what went wrong.

expected: there are three reasons for the decline in the reserve

feedback.why_key: There has no meaning of its own, so the verb looks forward to reasons and matches that.
feedback.feed_forward: After there, read on before you choose is or are.

payload.given: The findings are disputed. The findings come from a single study.
payload.instruction: Join them so that the second sentence sits inside the first as a relative clause.

expected: that come from a single study are disputed
which come from a single study are disputed
coming from a single study are disputed

feedback.why_key: Study is the last noun before the main verb but it is inside the clause, so are still answers to findings.
feedback.feed_forward: Bracket the relative clause off before you write the main verb.

payload.audio_text: The range of species recorded at the reserve has narrowed.

expected: the range of species recorded at the reserve has narrowed

feedback.why_key: Has is squashed almost to nothing in speech, and species gives no clue either way, so the head noun is the only guide.
feedback.feed_forward: Catch the head noun and let it predict the auxiliary.

items.decision_cue: The cost of these measures are

payload.sentence: The cost of these measures are passed straight on to households.

expected: is

neither cannot be used with two people
the verb should be plural because two parties are named
nothing wrong, it's fine

points.title: Knowing where one sentence stops and the next one starts

teach.can_do: I can tell where one sentence ends and stop it there with a mark strong enough to hold.
teach.why_it_matters: A broken boundary makes a reader go back and start the sentence again, and a reader who has to reread is the most expensive reader you can have.
teach.meaning: A clause with its own subject and its own finite verb can stand up alone: it is a whole sentence. English gives you four ways to put two of them together and a comma on its own is not one of them, because a comma is a pause inside a sentence rather than a join between two. Break it one way and you get a splice or a run-on. Break it the other way and you get a fragment, a piece that never stands up at all.

form.pattern: clause . clause · clause ; clause · clause , and/but/so/or + clause · subordinator + clause , clause
notes: however, therefore, moreover, for example and in addition are not joining words, so a comma in front of one leaves two whole sentences taped together
a semicolon is a full stop that promises the next sentence is closely related
a fragment is a piece with no subject, or no finite verb, or a subordinate clause left standing alone
two whole sentences with nothing at all between them is a run-on
and, but, so, or, yet and for are the only words that can sit beside the comma and take the weight
form.negative: Making one half negative changes nothing: the scheme was cheap, but it did not save anybody any time.
form.question: Ask of each half whether you could send it on its own and be understood.

left.text: The scheme cost forty million pounds

spec.caption: A comma is too light to hold these two apart. A full stop, a semicolon or a joining word can.

worked_example.sentence: The scheme cost forty million pounds, but it saved only nine minutes.
worked_example.why_this_form: Both halves stand up alone, so the comma needs a joining word beside it before it is strong enough to hold them apart.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: With the comma alone the reader is told to pause where they should have stopped, reaches the second subject, and has to go back to find where the new sentence began.

notice_set.sentence: The trial ran for six months. The results were never published.
notice_set.question: How many separate pieces of news are here?
notice_set.why: Each stretch stands up on its own, and the full stop between them says so.

notice_set.sentence: Although the funding was cut, the course finished on time.
notice_set.question: Did the course finish on time?
notice_set.why: Although makes the first half lean on the second, and the second half is the one making the claim.

notice_set.sentence: Because the funding was cut.
notice_set.question: Do we find out what happened?
notice_set.why: Because promises a main clause that never arrives, so the piece never gets round to saying anything.

notice_set.sentence: Fees rose, applications fell.
notice_set.question: Which of the two does the sentence say happened first?
notice_set.why: With nothing between them but a comma, the two facts are set down side by side with no order and no link.

notice_set.sentence: The trial ran for six months; the results were never published.
notice_set.question: Are the two facts offered as connected?
notice_set.why: A semicolon is a full stop that promises a connection, which is exactly the promise being made here.

teach.rule_line: If both halves could stand alone, a comma alone cannot hold them together.
teach.false_rule: That a run-on is a sentence that goes on too long. Length is not the fault; two whole sentences joined by a comma is.

errors.wrong: Online courses are cheaper, they also reach students in remote areas.
errors.right: Online courses are cheaper, and they also reach students in remote areas.
errors.why_it_happens: The two ideas arrive as one thought, and the comma is written to record that feeling. English marks the join with a word rather than with a pause.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: and, straight after the comma.
errors.l1_note: Several languages do allow a comma to join two clauses, so the habit transfers intact.

errors.wrong: The scheme was popular, however it was never funded.
errors.right: The scheme was popular, but it was never funded.
errors.why_it_happens: However is taught in a list of linking words, so it looks like it can carry a join. It links the meaning across a boundary but it cannot be the boundary.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: however becomes but.

errors.wrong: Fees rose again this year applications fell for the first time.
errors.right: Fees rose again this year, and applications fell for the first time.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer is thinking faster than they are punctuating, so the boundary is heard as a breath and never written down as a mark at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: and, where the breath falls.

errors.wrong: Schools cannot plan ahead. Because so many new teachers leave within five years.
errors.right: Schools cannot plan ahead, because so many new teachers leave within five years.
errors.why_it_happens: The piece feels complete because it answers the question the sentence before has just raised. On the page the question is gone and the answer has nothing left to hang on.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one mark: the full stop before because becomes a comma.

pays_in.model: Online courses are cheaper; they also reach students who cannot travel to a campus.

pays_in.note: A letter of complaint is a chain of short whole sentences, and each one has to close.
pays_in.model: The service was cancelled twice. On neither occasion was any notice given.

pays_in.note: Full stops and semicolons tell you where an argument turns.
pays_in.model: The trial ran for six months; the results were never published.

feedback.why_key: Although sets up a contrast with something, and the something never arrives, so nothing has actually been said.

the second half needs a joining word as well
the two halves should be one sentence with no mark

yet
although
though

feedback.why_key: The joining word sits exactly on the boundary, which is why the boundary stops being a problem.

the course is cheaper and it is open to people who cannot travel
the course is cheaper and its open to people who cant travel

feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the small word at the boundary and write it down first.

payload.sentence: Online courses are cheaper, they also reach students in remote areas.

cheaper, and they
cheaper. they
cheaper; they

items.decision_cue: popular, however it was never funded

popular but it was never funded

the two halves have been put in the wrong order

the town hall has been put in the wrong place

points.title: Putting commas where they earn their place

point_json.grammar_name: Comma rules: fronted adverbial, extra clause, list, and the comma that must not appear

teach.can_do: I can place a comma because of what the sentence is doing, not because of where I would breathe.
teach.why_it_matters: Two of the four comma jobs change what a sentence claims, so a stray pair can hand a reader a number or a group you never meant.
teach.meaning: A comma has four jobs and one thing it must never do. It closes a piece of scenery placed in front of the main clause. It fences off a clause or a phrase that is extra rather than identifying, with one comma each side. It separates the items of a list. And it stands beside and, but or so when two whole clauses are joined. What it may never do is stand between a subject and its verb, however long the subject has grown.

form.pattern: front matter , main clause · noun , extra news , verb · a , b and c · clause , and clause
notes: a phrase in front of the main clause closes with a comma: in most European cities, cycling has grown
an extra clause takes commas on both sides, and once you open the fence you must close it
no comma before a defining clause, because that clause is telling the reader which one you mean
in a list the comma before and is optional in British English, and whichever you choose you keep
no comma between a subject and its verb, however long the subject: what the survey actually showed was something else
form.negative: A negative main clause is punctuated the same way: after the first year, the trial was not extended.
form.question: In a question the front matter still closes with a comma: after the first year, was the trial extended?

left.role: scenery, which closes with a comma

right.role: the sentence itself, which never takes one before its verb

spec.caption: The comma marks where the scenery ends, not where you would take a breath.

worked_example.sentence: Since the paywall went up, the paper's local coverage, which had already been cut twice, has almost disappeared.
worked_example.why_this_form: The opening phrase is scenery and closes with a comma. The middle clause is extra news about coverage there is only one of, so it is fenced off on both sides.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Take the second pair of commas away and the clause starts identifying, which would claim there is some other local coverage that has not been cut.

notice_set.sentence: The reporters, who had covered the harbour, were moved to the news desk.
notice_set.question: Were all the reporters moved?
notice_set.why: The commas make the harbour a side note, so the sentence is about the whole group of reporters.

notice_set.sentence: The reporters who had covered the harbour were moved to the news desk.
notice_set.question: Were all the reporters moved?
notice_set.why: With no commas the clause picks a smaller group out of a bigger one, and only that group moved.

notice_set.sentence: After the paywall went up, sales fell for four months.
notice_set.question: Did sales fall before or after the paywall went up?
notice_set.why: The front phrase sets the time and the comma closes it, so everything after the comma sits inside that time.

notice_set.sentence: The paper covers sport, local politics and planning.
notice_set.question: How many areas does the paper cover?
notice_set.why: The comma and the final and mark off three separate items on one list.

notice_set.sentence: The editor who joined last year has already left.
notice_set.question: Has the paper had more than one editor recently?
notice_set.why: No commas means the clause is telling you which editor, and that only has a job to do if there was more than one.

teach.rule_line: A comma marks a boundary in the grammar, never a place to breathe.
teach.false_rule: That a comma goes wherever you would pause. Read a long subject aloud and you will pause; the comma still must not go there.

errors.wrong: Journalists, who work freelance, are paid for each piece.
errors.right: Journalists who work freelance are paid for each piece.
errors.why_it_happens: The clause feels like an aside, so it is fenced off out of politeness. The fence turns a claim about freelancers into a claim about every journalist alive.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete two marks: both commas.

errors.wrong: The scheme, which the council approved in March has already stalled.
errors.right: The scheme, which the council approved in March, has already stalled.
errors.why_it_happens: The opening comma goes in correctly and the writer then reads on through the clause and forgets that a fence needs a second side.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one mark: a comma after March.

errors.wrong: What the survey actually showed, was a sharp fall in trust.
errors.right: What the survey actually showed was a sharp fall in trust.
errors.why_it_happens: The subject has grown long enough that the writer needs a breath, and the mark is placed where the breath falls rather than where the grammar allows one.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one mark: the comma.

errors.wrong: In most European cities cycling to work has grown sharply.
errors.right: In most European cities, cycling to work has grown sharply.
errors.why_it_happens: The opening phrase is short enough to read smoothly without a mark, so nothing warns the writer that a reader has to guess where the scenery ends.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one mark: a comma after cities.

pays_in.note: Fronted phrases and extra clauses are how a body paragraph varies its shape.
pays_in.model: In most large cities, local reporting, which used to be funded by advertising, has thinned out.

pays_in.note: Every trend sentence opens with a time phrase that has to close.
pays_in.model: Between 2015 and 2019, the share of readers under thirty fell by half.

pays_in.note: A pair of commas tells you the clause inside is not narrowing anything down.
pays_in.model: The trial, which ran for six months, was never repeated.

used_in.quote: Answers on this prompt lean on fronted time phrases and on extra clauses about the newspapers themselves.

feedback.why_key: The commas fence the clause off as a side note, so the sentence is about the whole group and being freelance is extra.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a fenced clause as extra news, never as a filter.

payload.sentence: The photographers who were freelance were paid a month late.
payload.question: Were all the photographers paid late?

feedback.why_key: With the fence gone the clause narrows the group, so the staff photographers were paid on time.
feedback.feed_forward: Count who is left outside the clause when there are no commas.

payload.sentence: Between 2015 and 2019, the number of cycle journeys almost doubled.
reasons: the front phrase should not take a comma
a second comma is needed before the verb
the years should come at the end
nothing wrong, it's fine

payload.context: There is one paper in Marlow, and the fence is already in place around the clause.
payload.stem: The Marlow paper, ___ has covered the harbour since 1954, is closing in June.

expected: which

feedback.why_key: Inside a pair of commas the clause is extra news, and that is the one place where that cannot stand.

payload.context: Open the paragraph with a phrase that sets the place before the claim arrives.
payload.stem: ___ most European cities, cycling to work has grown steadily.

expected: in

feedback.why_key: The phrase is scenery placed in front of the sentence, and the comma after cities is what tells the reader the scenery has ended.

payload.context: Build one sentence that opens with the time and then makes the claim.

expected: after the paywall went up local sales fell sharply

feedback.why_key: The mark belongs at the join between the scenery and the sentence, which is after up and nowhere else.

the editor who's been there since 2019 is leaving in june
the editor who has been there since 2019 is leaving in june

payload.context: From a draft paragraph about a council planning decision.
payload.sentence: The scheme, which the council approved in March has already stalled.
reasons: the fence round the extra clause has only one side
which should be that
the date has been put in the wrong place

payload.context: Two lines from different letters about the same college.
sentences: The tutors who trained abroad run the evening classes.
The tutors, who trained abroad, run the evening classes.

points.title: The rest of the marks: semicolon, colon, apostrophe and capital letter

point_json.grammar_name: Semicolon, colon, apostrophe, capitalisation and quotation

teach.can_do: I can use a semicolon, a colon and an apostrophe for what each of them actually does.
teach.why_it_matters: These are the cheapest marks on the page: each error is one character, each is instantly visible, and none of them takes any thought once the job is named.
teach.meaning: A semicolon is a full stop that promises the next sentence is closely related, so what stands on either side of it must be a whole sentence. A colon announces that what follows is the thing just promised: an example, a list, an explanation. An apostrophe does two jobs only, belonging and a missing letter, and it never marks more than one. Capital letters belong to names, not to words that feel important.

form.pattern: clause ; clause · clause : the thing announced · noun + 's = belonging · it's = it is
notes: a semicolon needs a whole sentence on each side; a comma there is a splice
a colon needs a whole sentence in front of it, and can be followed by a list, a phrase or a clause
its means belonging to it; it's means it is or it has
plurals never take an apostrophe: the 1990s, three CVs, two buses
a plural owner takes the apostrophe after the s: the residents' committee
capitals go on people, places, institutions, months and days, not on subjects or job titles in general
form.negative: A negative second half changes none of it: the shop reopened in May; the owners have not taken a wage since.
form.question: A question can follow a colon: the report asks one thing: can the street survive another year?

spec.caption: If the word is only counting, it takes no mark at all.

worked_example.sentence: The firm's accounts were filed late: its finance team had lost three weeks to a software change.
worked_example.why_this_form: The first mark shows the accounts belong to the firm. The colon announces the explanation that was promised, and its is the belonging form, which never takes a mark.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: It's finance team would read as it is finance team, and a semicolon in place of the colon would drop the promise that a reason is on its way.

notice_set.sentence: The shop's owner has appealed against the decision.
notice_set.question: How many shops are being talked about?
notice_set.why: The mark sits in front of the s, and that is where English puts it when the owner is a single thing.

notice_set.sentence: The shops' owner has appealed against the decision.
notice_set.question: How many shops are being talked about?
notice_set.why: The mark has moved behind the s, which is what happens once the owner is already a group.

notice_set.sentence: Its front window was replaced last month.
notice_set.question: Whose window was replaced?
options: Somebody who has not been named
notice_set.why: Its with no mark means belonging, and what it belongs to is whatever the writing was already about.

notice_set.sentence: The report gives one reason: rents.
notice_set.question: How many reasons are given?
notice_set.why: The colon delivers exactly what the sentence in front of it promised, and one reason was promised.

notice_set.sentence: Sales fell every quarter; the owners blamed the new car park.
notice_set.question: Are the two facts offered as connected?
notice_set.why: A semicolon stops the first sentence and promises that the second belongs with it.

teach.rule_line: An apostrophe means belonging or a missing letter, and never means more than one.
teach.false_rule: That an apostrophe tidies up an s. Plurals never take one, not for decades, not for initials, not for prices.

errors.wrong: Its important to compare prices before buying anything large.
errors.right: It's important to compare prices before buying anything large.
errors.why_it_happens: The two sound identical, and everywhere else in English the belonging form is the one that carries the mark, so the mark is dropped exactly where it is needed.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one mark: an apostrophe in its.

points.title: The prepositions that belong to a word and travel with it

point_json.grammar_name: Dependent prepositions on verbs, adjectives and nouns

teach.can_do: I can keep the right preposition attached to a word instead of guessing at it.
teach.why_it_matters: It is scored under vocabulary as often as under grammar, and it is one of the few errors that survives every other improvement a learner makes.
teach.meaning: Some prepositions are not chosen at all. They arrive attached to a particular word and stay with it wherever it goes: depend on, result in, aware of, an increase in, a solution to. No rule predicts which one, because the preposition is not being used for its meaning here. It is part of the word. That is why these are learned as pairs, inside sentences, the way a phrase is learned, rather than reasoned out at the moment of writing.

form.pattern: verb + its own preposition · adjective + its own preposition · noun + its own preposition
notes: the verb and the noun for one idea often disagree: it affects prices, but an effect on prices
the family usually keeps its preposition: depend on, dependent on, dependence on
a preposition is always followed by a noun or an -ing form: aware of losing, never aware of lose
an increase in names what is rising; an increase of names the size of the rise
some words take a preposition in one meaning and none in another: discuss the plan, but an argument about the plan
form.negative: The pair holds together under negation: the outcome does not depend on the weather.
form.question: The preposition stays with its word even when the question word moves: what does the outcome depend on?

right.role: the preposition that came with it

spec.caption: Store the two boxes as one item. Splitting them is what creates the error.

worked_example.sentence: The rise in flooding results from decades of drainage work upstream.
worked_example.why_this_form: Rise brings in with it and results brings from with it. Neither preposition is describing a place or a time; each one belongs to its word.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Rise of would push the reader towards the size of the change, and results in would turn the sentence round and make the drainage the outcome.

notice_set.sentence: Rainfall in the catchment rose by twelve per cent.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence tell us the figure it reached?
notice_set.why: By gives the size of the change and leaves the level it arrived at unstated.

notice_set.sentence: Rainfall in the catchment rose to twelve inches.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence tell us the figure it reached?
notice_set.why: To names the point the line arrived at, which is exactly the figure.

notice_set.sentence: The flooding resulted from years of drainage work.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: Result from looks backwards to the cause, so the drainage is the earlier of the two.

notice_set.sentence: Local groups are concerned about the river.
notice_set.question: Are the groups worried?
notice_set.why: Concerned about is worried; concerned with would only mean the river is what they work on.

notice_set.sentence: There has been a sharp increase in reported spills.
notice_set.question: Is the number of spills going up?
notice_set.why: Increase brings in with it, and whatever follows in is the thing that is rising.

teach.rule_line: Learn the preposition with the word, inside a sentence, never as a rule.
teach.false_rule: That you can work the preposition out from what it means. Here it carries no meaning of its own.

errors.wrong: The outcome depends of the weather in early spring.
errors.right: The outcome depends on the weather in early spring.
errors.why_it_happens: Of is the commonest preposition in the language and gets reached for as a default whenever the required one was never stored beside the verb.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: of becomes on.

errors.wrong: Rising temperatures have an effect in crop yields.
errors.right: Rising temperatures have an effect on crop yields.
errors.why_it_happens: The verb affect takes no preposition at all, so the learner's memory of the idea offers no clue about what the noun form demands.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: in becomes on.

errors.wrong: The council is aware about the state of the river.
errors.right: The council is aware of the state of the river.
errors.why_it_happens: About is the preposition for a topic and awareness does have a topic, so the wrong choice is the semantically reasonable one.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: about becomes of.

errors.wrong: There is no solution for this without national funding.
errors.right: There is no solution to this without national funding.
errors.why_it_happens: For marks purpose and a solution obviously has a purpose, which makes the wrong preposition the more logical of the two on the page.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: for becomes to.

pays_in.note: Rise in, rise by and rise to sit in almost every line of a data description.
pays_in.model: The increase in household demand was matched by a fall in industrial use.

pays_in.note: Depend on, result in and contribute to carry most causal sentences.
pays_in.model: Much of the damage results from decisions taken thirty years ago.

pays_in.note: Part 3 answers are built on aware of, worried about and responsible for.
pays_in.model: Most people are aware of the problem, but very few feel responsible for it.

feedback.why_key: By gives the size of the step and says nothing about where the line started or finished.
feedback.feed_forward: Read by as the size of the change.

payload.sentence: The damage resulted from three decades of drainage work.
payload.question: Which happened first?

feedback.why_key: Result from looks backwards to the cause, so whatever follows from is the earlier event.
feedback.feed_forward: Let from and in tell you which way the causing runs.

payload.context: A Part 3 answer about who should pay for cleaning up rivers.
payload.sentence: Most people are aware of the problem but nobody wants to pay for it.
reasons: aware takes about rather than of
pay takes no preposition at all
the two halves need a different joining word
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Aware brings of with it and pay brings for with it, and both pairs are sitting intact.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the preposition against the word in front of it, not the word after.

payload.context: From an essay paragraph about flood defences.
payload.stem: How well the scheme works depends ___ how much rain falls in March.

expected: on
upon

feedback.why_key: Depend carries on with it wherever it goes, in every tense and in every word class in its family.
feedback.feed_forward: Store depend on as one item, never as two.

payload.context: The opening line of a description of a line graph.
payload.stem: The graph shows a steady increase ___ the number of recorded spills.

expected: in

feedback.why_key: Increase brings in with it, and what follows in is the thing that is going up rather than the size of the rise.
feedback.feed_forward: Write an increase in whenever you name what is rising.

payload.context: From a paragraph arguing that the problem has no cheap answer.
payload.stem: There is no realistic solution ___ this without national funding.

expected: to

feedback.why_key: Solution takes to, even though a solution has a purpose and for would be the more logical guess.
feedback.feed_forward: Learn solution to as one word with a gap in the middle.

payload.given: Rising temperatures affect crop yields across the region.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so that the verb becomes a noun.

expected: an effect on crop yields across the region
an effect on crop yields

feedback.why_key: The verb needs no preposition and the noun demands one, which is why the two forms of the same idea have to be stored separately.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the preposition again every time you change word class.

payload.audio_text: It's led to a rise in flooding and a fall in water quality.

expected: it's led to a rise in flooding and a fall in water quality
it has led to a rise in flooding and a fall in water quality
its led to a rise in flooding and a fall in water quality

feedback.why_key: Every one of these prepositions is unstressed, so what you catch is the word in front of it and what you write is whatever was stored beside that word.
feedback.feed_forward: Catch the noun, then write the preposition it always takes.

payload.sentence: The council has been aware about the state of the river since 2019.

expected: aware of

feedback.why_key: About is what you would choose from the meaning, and aware simply does not take it.
feedback.feed_forward: Trust the stored pair over the meaning.

the sentence needs a different tense

feedback.feed_forward: Write the pair as one unit before you finish the sentence.

feedback.feed_forward: Underline every preposition and name the word it belongs to.

points.title: Saying where, when and how with a small package of words

point_json.grammar_name: Prepositional phrases as adverbials, and where they sit

teach.can_do: I can build a phrase that says where, when or how, and put it where English keeps it.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the cheapest way to make a short sentence longer without adding a clause, and misplacing one is the most audible word-order error there is.
teach.meaning: A preposition plus a noun makes a small package that behaves like a single word: along the coast path, in the summer, without much warning, for three days. The package can say where, when, how, why or how long, and it can sit at the end of the clause or be moved to the front to set the scene. The one place it can never sit is between a verb and the thing that verb acts on.

form.pattern: subject + verb + object + how + where + when
notes: the default order at the end is manner, then place, then time: the coach left quietly from the square at six
moving a package to the front makes it the setting for what follows, and it closes with a comma
nothing may stand between a verb and its object: we visited the museum on Tuesday, never we visited on Tuesday the museum
two packages of the same kind go smaller first: at nine on Friday, in a village near the coast
some verbs demand a particular preposition: we arrived at the village, never arrived to it
form.negative: The package sits in the same place in a negative clause: the path was not open in February.
form.question: It also stays put in a question: did the path close in February?

left.role: the verb and its object, which stay welded together

right.role: the package, which waits its turn

spec.caption: Nothing gets in between the verb and the thing it acts on.

worked_example.sentence: The coach drops walkers at the old harbour every morning in summer.
worked_example.why_this_form: The object comes straight after the verb, then the place package, then the two time packages with the smaller one first.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Putting every morning in front of walkers would split the verb from what it acts on, and the reader would stall halfway through the action waiting for the object.

notice_set.sentence: The coast path was closed for three days.
notice_set.question: Do we know when it was closed?
notice_set.why: For gives the length of the closure and never says which three days they were.

notice_set.sentence: The coast path was closed on the third of March.
notice_set.question: Do we know how long it was closed?
notice_set.why: On names a point in the calendar, and a point has no length to report.

notice_set.sentence: Walkers reached the village along the old coast path.
notice_set.question: Which route did they take?
notice_set.why: The package answers where, and it answers it by naming the route rather than the destination.

notice_set.sentence: Without much warning, the ferry stopped running in October.
notice_set.question: Did people know in advance?
notice_set.why: The fronted package sets the conditions for everything that follows it.

notice_set.sentence: Buses run twice a day in summer.
notice_set.question: Do buses run twice a day in winter?
notice_set.why: In summer fences the claim into one season and leaves the rest of the year entirely unmentioned.

teach.rule_line: Keep the verb and its object together, then add how, where and when.
teach.false_rule: That these phrases can go anywhere because they are extra. They move freely except into the gap after a verb.

errors.wrong: We visited on the Tuesday the harbour museum.
errors.right: We visited the harbour museum on the Tuesday.
errors.why_it_happens: The day feels like the point of the sentence, so it is said as soon as the verb is out. English guards the space after a verb for the object alone.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one phrase: on the Tuesday goes to the end.
errors.l1_note: Languages with freer word order allow exactly this, so the habit arrives fully formed.

errors.wrong: The ferry runs in summer from the old harbour.
errors.right: The ferry runs from the old harbour in summer.
errors.why_it_happens: The two packages come out in the order they were thought of rather than in the fixed English order, which puts place in front of time.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap two phrases: the place one goes first.

errors.wrong: We arrived to the village well after dark.
errors.right: We arrived at the village well after dark.
errors.why_it_happens: Arrive describes movement towards a place and to is the movement preposition, which makes the wrong choice the more reasonable one.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: to becomes at.

errors.wrong: We went last August to the northern islands.
errors.right: We went to the northern islands last August.
errors.why_it_happens: The time is the news, so it is placed as early as possible. A verb of movement still wants its destination beside it before anything else arrives.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one phrase: last August goes to the end.

pays_in.note: A two-minute story is mostly packages saying where and when.
pays_in.model: We set off from the harbour just after seven, in absolutely flat weather.

pays_in.note: A letter changing arrangements is a chain of place and time packages.
pays_in.model: I will be at the ferry terminal from four o'clock on the Friday.

pays_in.note: A map description is nothing but position packages.
pays_in.model: A car park was built on the far side of the bay, behind the dunes.

feedback.feed_forward: Read for as a length and on as a point.

payload.sentence: Without any warning, the coast path was closed to walkers.
payload.question: Did walkers know in advance?

feedback.why_key: The fronted package sets the conditions before the sentence starts, so everything after it happened under those conditions.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a fronted package as the setting for what follows.

feedback.why_key: A side is a surface you spread across, so the package that names it opens with on.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the preposition to the shape of the place.

payload.context: Say when you set off on the last day.

expected: we left the hostel at seven on the friday

feedback.why_key: The object comes first, then the two time packages with the smaller unit in front of the bigger one.
feedback.feed_forward: Order two time packages smaller first.

expected: the ferry runs from the old harbour in summer

feedback.why_key: Place comes before time whenever both are sitting at the end of the clause.
feedback.feed_forward: Say where before you say when.

payload.audio_text: We'd walked the whole path by the middle of the afternoon.

expected: we'd walked the whole path by the middle of the afternoon
we had walked the whole path by the middle of the afternoon

feedback.why_key: By opens a package that names a deadline rather than a duration, and it is squashed to almost nothing in speech.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the small word that opens each package.

payload.error_span: visited on the Tuesday the harbour museum

expected: visited the harbour museum on the tuesday
on the tuesday we visited the harbour museum

points.title: Where an adverb goes, and the one place it must never stand

point_json.grammar_name: Adverb placement: mid-position, end-position and what may not be split

teach.can_do: I can place an adverb where English keeps it, and I know which two adverbs change the claim when they move.
teach.why_it_matters: A misplaced adverb is heard as a mistake immediately, and with only and even it does not just sound wrong, it says something else.
teach.meaning: English keeps three positions open for an adverb: in front of the clause, in the middle just before the main verb, and at the end. Choosing between them mostly moves the emphasis rather than the meaning. There is one large exception: only and even attach to whatever stands straight after them, so moving one of those moves the claim itself. And there is one closed position, the gap between a verb and its object, which nothing at all may occupy.

form.pattern: front , clause · subject + adverb + main verb · clause + adverb
notes: mid-position is before the main verb, but after be and after the first auxiliary: she is rarely late, she has never driven
adverbs of manner and definite time go at the end: he explained it clearly, the results came back yesterday
nothing goes between a verb and its object: I liked the idea very much, never I liked very much the idea
only and even go immediately in front of the words they are about
probably, certainly and definitely take mid-position, and in a negative they come before not: she probably will not agree
form.negative: In a negative, a frequency adverb goes after not: she has not always worked nights.
form.question: In a question the adverb stays behind the subject: has she ever worked nights?

worked_example.sentence: Patients rarely mention the cost, and staff almost never raise it either.
worked_example.why_this_form: Both adverbs sit in mid-position, immediately before the main verb, which is where frequency lives when there is no auxiliary to follow.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Patients mention rarely the cost would split the verb from what it acts on, and the reader would stall on rarely still waiting for the object.

notice_set.sentence: Only the night staff were told about the change.
notice_set.question: Were the day staff told?
notice_set.why: Only attaches to what comes straight after it, so the night staff are the whole of the group that heard.

notice_set.sentence: The night staff were only told about the change.
notice_set.question: Were the night staff asked what they thought?
notice_set.why: Only has moved onto told, so telling is the whole of what happened to them.

notice_set.sentence: She has never worked a night shift.
notice_set.question: Has she worked nights at some point?
notice_set.why: Never sits after the auxiliary and empties her whole working life of night shifts.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic almost always runs late.
notice_set.question: Does the clinic ever run on time?
notice_set.why: Almost pulls always back from the edge, which leaves a few days when it does not run late.

notice_set.sentence: Even the consultants were asked to fill in the form.
notice_set.question: Was anybody else asked?
notice_set.why: Even marks the consultants as the surprising addition, which only makes sense if others came first.

teach.rule_line: Nothing may stand between a verb and its object, not even one short adverb.
teach.false_rule: That an adverb goes next to the word it describes. It describes the verb and still may not sit between the verb and its object.

errors.wrong: I like very much this approach to prevention.
errors.right: I like this approach to prevention very much.
errors.why_it_happens: Very much feels like part of the liking, so it is written straight after the verb. English keeps that space for the object and nothing else.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one phrase: very much goes to the end.
errors.l1_note: Many languages place the degree phrase directly after the verb, and the habit transfers whole.

errors.wrong: She goes always to the clinic on a Friday.
errors.right: She always goes to the clinic on a Friday.
errors.why_it_happens: The adverb is placed where most languages keep it, immediately after the verb, and nothing in the meaning of the sentence protests.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: always goes in front of goes.

errors.wrong: He has worked never at the weekend.
errors.right: He has never worked at the weekend.
errors.why_it_happens: Mid-position has been stored as after the verb rather than as after the first auxiliary, so the adverb lands one word too late.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: never goes after has.

errors.wrong: The results came back probably on Thursday.
errors.right: The results probably came back on Thursday.
errors.why_it_happens: Probably is being treated as a comment on the day, so it is written beside the day. It is a comment on the whole sentence and lives in mid-position.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: probably goes in front of came.

pays_in.note: Frequency adverbs are unavoidable in answers about routine.
pays_in.model: I hardly ever go to the gym in winter, but I usually walk to work.

pays_in.note: Hedging words live in mid-position, and a misplaced one reads as a slip.
pays_in.model: Governments rarely fund prevention as generously as treatment.

pays_in.note: Where only sits decides what a sentence is actually claiming.
pays_in.model: Only two of the six trials reported any change in daily activity.

feedback.why_key: Only attaches to the words straight after it, so the evening clinic is the whole of what was cancelled.
feedback.feed_forward: Read only forwards, never backwards.

payload.question: Was the evening clinic moved to another day?

feedback.why_key: Only has moved onto cancelled, so cancelling is the whole of what was done and nothing was rearranged.

payload.context: The clinic runs late on nearly every day, but not on every single one.
payload.stem: The clinic ___ (almost / always) runs behind by mid-morning.

expected: almost always

feedback.why_key: Almost softens always, so it has to stand in front of it; reversed, the pair would say something no speaker means.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the softening word in front of the one it softens.

feedback.feed_forward: Name the position before you write the adverb.
